title: Vendor-neutral body-cam redaction bureau with fee pass-through
one_liner: A CJIS-cleared remote team that returns double-reviewed redacted police video priced per minute below the fee small cities already charge requesters, so the bureau funds itself.
customer: Small police departments and sheriff's offices (roughly 5-60 sworn officers) with records backlogs, and the city clerks and attorneys who carry the liability. They pay $0.40-0.60 per video minute plus a small monthly minimum.
problem: Small agencies do not have redaction staff. Elko, NV's police chief described about a year of catching up on redaction requests with no full-time redaction team and approved a five-year Axon extension of about $91,200 a year. White Salmon, WA has only two trained employees and set a $0.84-per-minute redaction fee (4-1 vote, April 15, 2026) while the chief said he 'cannot readily add a second-review step for all releases' because of limited trained staff and high request volume. A councilor dissented, arguing that sensitive footage such as juveniles needs more than one reviewer. Phoenix has nearly 40,000 pending public-records requests and raised commercial fees to pay for staff. AI-generated request floods (Somerset County, PA saw dozens a day) make it worse.
solution: A regional redaction bureau. Departments send only the clips requested (through share links from Axon, Motorola/WatchGuard, Getac and Wolfcom or others) and get back redacted video plus a redaction log within 5 business days. Automated face, plate and audio detection does the first pass. Then two trained human reviewers sign off, with a state-specific checklist (juveniles, victims, medical, informants). The bureau also sells 'backlog amnesty sprints' at a flat rate to clear a year-old queue. Vendor neutrality is the selling point, since Axon's automated redaction only helps agencies inside its ecosystem and still requires manual verification.
why_now: Body camera adoption is nearly universal after 2025-2026 contract cycles (Elko, Plainview, Crescent City, Carlsbad, Kasson approvals), public-records volume is up, and states are formalizing per-minute cost recovery. Councils are now adopting the fee schedules that make a pass-through model possible.
revenue_model: Per-minute fee ($0.40-0.60) billed to the agency, which recovers most or all of it from requesters at its own per-minute fee (White Salmon: $0.84); monthly minimum of $250; flat-rate backlog sprints of $5k-20k.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not blurring speed, it is a defensible second review on sensitive content, which small departments cannot staff. The fee schedule councils are adopting is derived from a cost-of-service study, so the department can pass the bureau's cost straight through; the bureau's margin lies between its price and the city's published fee. CJIS clearance and background checks form the moat that keeps generic video-AI startups out. Evidence: Elko's year-long backlog (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog); White Salmon's two trained employees, the $0.84/minute fee and the second-review dissent (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8492326/washington/klickitat-county/white-salmon/council-updates-public-records-policy-approves-084-per-minute-body-camera-redaction-fee-over-staff-objections); Phoenix's roughly 40,000 pending requests (https://www.kjzz.org/politics/2026-09-24/commercial-public-records-requests-prices-have-gone-up-in-phoenix-in-effort-to-hire-more-staff).
first_30_days: Pick one state, such as Washington, with strong public-records laws and many small departments. Sign the CJIS security addendum with 2 agencies and have all reviewers fingerprint-cleared. Find 15 departments with a visible backlog in recent council minutes and offer a flat 'backlog amnesty sprint' on their first 500 minutes at $0.45/min. Turn the state's checklist into a review template and deliver the first 3 jobs within the month.

title: Data Centers That Make Water From Waste Heat
one_liner: Containerized membrane-distillation skids that use a liquid-cooled data center's own warm return loop to turn cooling-tower blowdown or brackish well water into clean make-up water.
customer: Colo and AI-hosting operators in Texas, Arizona and Nevada facing water audits, plus immersion-cooled bitcoin and HPC hosts whose loops run hot. Operators buy or lease; fabs later.
problem: Data centers are the target of water regulation (Texas freeze and reporting crime, Australian standards, New York and Ohio actions), and cooling blowdown creates a discharge headache. Desalination was uneconomic because heat was expensive, but a data center produces heat it must remove anyway.
solution: Integrate membrane-distillation modules from an existing OEM with the site's warm loop (liquid-cooled racks now return water at roughly 45-65 C, my estimate). The skid concentrates blowdown and produces distillate for make-up water, cutting purchased water and discharge volume. Add a metering-and-ledger layer that produces a verified 'water-negative' claim. First product: a 10-50 m3/day skid.
why_now: A 2025 Chinese plant reported desal near $0.28/m3 using waste heat (not fully verified). Liquid cooling is spreading, and regulators and lenders now ask for verified water use.
revenue_model: $250-600k equipment sale per skid, or water-as-a-service at roughly $1.5-3/m3 plus O&M. Regulatory value (fewer permits, less discharge) is the closing argument.
non_obvious_insight: Membrane distillation lost to reverse osmosis because it needs large amounts of heat, and a data center offers abundant heat that must be removed, so its energy cost is effectively negative. The villain of the water story becomes the equipment that solves it.
first_30_days: Find three immersion-cooled mining or HPC hosts in Texas with 55-65 C loops. Partner with an MD module OEM for a 5 m3/day trial unit ($60-120k). Sign an LOI with a host for a 90-day pilot that shares data on kWh-thermal per m3, TDS and fouling.

title: Patent-Grade Variant Maps for Biologics
one_liner: Pooled-screening service that generates the sequence-function data biologics patents now need after Amgen v. Sanofi, plus a mirror-image design-around report for companies facing sequence claims.
customer: IP counsel and patent boutiques at antibody and protein biotechs, biosimilar and biobetter developers, and mid-size biotechs working in crowded target classes.
problem: Trend chain: Amgen v. Sanofi (2023) killed functional genus antibody claims unless the specification enables the full scope. Patents therefore shrink toward sequence-specific claims backed by data. Counsel typically has data on 20-50 variants. Meanwhile cheap DNA and AI design make thousands of function-preserving variants easy to produce, so both breadth-by-data (offense) and design-around (defense) become experimental problems that no one packages.
solution: Offense: pooled display or mammalian screening of 10^4-10^6 designed variants with NGS readout, delivered as patent-ready sequence-function tables and generalizations (which CDR positions tolerate what) to support broader claims. Defense: search patent sequence claims, compute identity against claim thresholds, design function-preserving escapes and validate the top candidates in a pool. Sold through IP counsel, not legal advice.
why_now: DNA is no longer the cost: Weizmann built 2.5 billion antibody fragments on phage for EUR 38,000 of DNA. Zero-shot design tools generate variants at scale. Post-Amgen enablement pressure has had three years to bite, and law-firm commentary is now explicitly tackling AI and enablement.
revenue_model: $40-150k per patent family for offense work, $8-25k per FTO or design-around candidate, and subscriptions for boutiques.
non_obvious_insight: With cheap DNA and pooled assays, 'enablement by data' becomes a commodity for whoever runs the experiment. Patent breadth turns into a function of wet-lab throughput rather than lawyer cleverness. The same machine that broadens your claims also narrows a competitor's, so buyers exist on both sides of every thicket.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IP boutiques as design partners. Build a claim-matching tool on public USPTO and EPO sequence listings. Offer 10 free FTO scans. Contract a pooled-display partner. Price one paid offense pilot with a biotech preparing a continuation filing.

title: The Recorder's Rulebook: Avalara for the Recording Counter
one_liner: A verified, machine-readable rulebook and fee oracle for every recording jurisdiction, with a preflight checker that tells you a document will be rejected before you send it.
customer: Small and mid-size title and escrow agencies, estate-planning and real estate attorneys, HOA and property managers, lenders' closing teams, and later closing-software and e-recording platforms that embed the API. Counties get listed free.
problem: There are roughly 3,600 recording jurisdictions, each with its own margins, font sizes, notary wording, parcel-ID format, cover sheets, per-page fees, surcharges and transfer taxes. Those rules sit on stale county web pages and in clerks' heads. Rejections delay closings two to seven days, burn recorder staff time on every bounce, and wrong fee estimates create TRID tolerance problems for lenders. Fees also keep moving as counties backfill shrinking recording revenue (Wayne County MI has floated a $30 fee increase, Montana raised per-page fees, and other counties report seven-figure losses tied to fee changes).
solution: A crowd-verified rulebook per county and document type. A PDF preflight scans geometry (margins, fonts, blank space), notary block completeness, legal description, APN format and preparer and return-to fields, and returns specific fixes. A to-the-penny fee and transfer-tax calculator handles every surcharge. A change log tracks statute changes and effective dates (many take effect July 1 or January 1). Each county gets a one-click quarterly 'attest my page' link, which clerks will use because every rejection costs them 15-30 minutes plus postage. Start as a free 'will this be rejected?' web checker to collect users, then sell API access.
why_now: Recording volumes have been depressed since 2022 and counties are raising fees, which makes fee tables stale. Remote online notarization and e-recording put far more documents in front of closers who have never met the county's quirks. Title staff attrition means fewer people who just know the rules. Vision-capable LLMs make geometry and notary-block checks cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: $1-$3 per preflight check plus $99-$499/month tiers for agencies. Per-call API pricing for closing platforms and e-recording vendors, and a data license for lenders needing accurate recording-fee and transfer-tax estimates.
non_obvious_insight: Clerks reject because the stamp is a legal act, not because we are picky. The top ten rejection reasons are identical everywhere, but the thresholds differ, and most bounces come from occasional submitters (attorneys, HOA managers, individuals), not the big title companies that already have local runners. The moat is not software, it is the boring verified dataset, and clerks will help you build it because they are the ones who suffer from the bounces.
first_30_days: Pick one state with an active recorders' association and build the full rulebook for 25 counties by phone and web, with a clerk sign-off on each. Ship the free checker, promote it through the association newsletter and estate-planning attorney groups, and convert the heaviest users to a $99/month plan. Approach a closing-software partner program once you have about 200 active users.

title: Referee Pathway: Officiating as a School Credential
one_liner: A semester-long, credit-bearing officiating course that puts teens in mentored cohorts on paid youth games, fixing the referee shortage by fixing retention.
customer: District CTE directors and state high-school athletic associations are the buyers. Youth leagues and game assignors are paying placement partners. Students (14+ where state rules allow) are the beneficiaries.
problem: Youth and high-school games are shortened or cancelled for lack of officials. Widely cited surveys say most new officials quit within two years, largely because of abuse from parents and fans. Meanwhile teens lack decent first jobs, entry-level white-collar hiring has cracked, and districts are chasing CTE pathways that lead to real work.
solution: A CTE elective, 'Officiating and Conflict Management'. Students learn rules, mechanics, film review and de-escalation role-play. They then work mentored, paid assignments as a cohort (never alone) at rec-league games, with body-worn cameras or comms for protection. The output is a portable 'Registered Official' credential aligned with the state association's licensing. We sell curriculum, assignment scheduling and an insurance wrapper.
why_now: The officials shortage has persisted since COVID and many states have passed laws penalizing assault on officials. CTE enrollment is rising (vocational-heavy public two-years grew 11.7% in Spring 2025). After the entry-level AI job shock, schools and parents want credentials tied to human judgment. Sports is one of the few settings where judgment under pressure is the actual job.
revenue_model: $150-300 per student license paid by districts from CTE budgets. An 8-10% platform fee on paid assignments (typically $40-80 per game). State-association sponsorships and body-cam/insurance partner rebates. A 40-student district cohort is roughly $8-12k plus assignment fees.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a retention problem caused by isolation and abuse in an official's first 20 games, not a recruiting problem. A school cohort is the only structure that gives new officials a team, a mentor and institutional backing. De-escalating under hostile scrutiny is also a transferable credential for security, hospitality, HR and healthcare jobs.
first_30_days: Pitch 2-3 CTE directors and the local officials' association. Run a 10-12 week after-school pilot for 30 students, funded by a rec league or booster at about $99 per student. Track how many are still officiating a season later against the roughly 20% baseline. Use the retention data and a league letter of support to pitch the state association.

title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.
non_obvious_insight: Percent complete is the wrong metric. The last 5% of a data center can consume 25% of the calendar, and it is dominated by unbounded tasks: the commissioning punch-list burn-down rate and whether the OEM has a startup technician free that month predict RFS far better than construction progress. You can only read those signals if you have run an IST. Also, the RFS date on a marketing sheet is a sales number, not a schedule.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and a teardown of one publicly delayed project. Approach 5-10 private credit and infrastructure funds with data center or GPU-lending desks. Offer a fixed-fee $25K second opinion on one live deal, delivered in two weeks, and ask permission to reference the engagement anonymously.

title: Second-Opinion Price Check for Vet Estimates
one_liner: Upload a photo of a vet estimate and get a line-by-line price benchmark and a list of questions to ask your vet within 24 hours, from vet-tech reviewers, for $19-29.
customer: Pet owners facing $500+ estimates (about 95M US households own pets), plus pet insurers and employers as a later benefit channel and independent clinics as a fair-price badge buyer.
problem: Vet services inflation ran 5.5% YoY in April 2026, and household spending at vets rose almost 4x as fast as spending on pet food and treats (about 1%). BofA Global Research says veterinary pricing is rising faster than wages, so many households delay wellness visits, dentistry and diagnostics. 25-30% of US veterinary practices, and roughly 75% of specialty clinics, are now owned by corporations or private equity (AVMA 2024, cited by BofA), which can erode competition. Pet insurance uptake stays low, and younger and lower-income households are pulling back on pet spending. When an owner is holding an estimate for a sick animal, there is no neutral benchmark.
solution: A mobile-first upload flow. OCR reads the estimate, and licensed vet techs (not diagnosing, just reviewing) compare each line item to regional price ranges, flag bundled or optional items, note which items are typically deferrable versus urgent, and give a short script of questions for the clinic. Every review adds anonymized line-item prices to a growing regional price database, which becomes the moat. Later features are a 'fair-price verified' badge for independent clinics and a payment-plan and generic-drug price check.
why_now: The data now shows a sharp split: sticker prices climb while pet food and store spending stalls, meaning owners are squeezed specifically at the vet. Private-equity consolidation is a live news story, and owners can share estimate photos easily. Pet-insurance carriers face rising claim costs and have an incentive to fund price transparency.
revenue_model: $19-29 per review, $9/month for unlimited pet-family plan, B2B licenses to insurers and employers ($1-3 per covered pet per month), and clinic subscriptions for verified fair-price badges ($99-199/month per clinic).
non_obvious_insight: The pain is not that pet care costs money, it is information asymmetry at the moment of an estimate, and the same dynamic is what made medical-bill advocacy a business for humans. Vet inflation is running roughly 4x pet-food spending growth, and owners are already responding by deferring care rather than shopping around, so the demand is for a fast, trusted benchmark, not another directory. Evidence: BofA Institute, 'The price of pet parenting has gone off leash,' 18 May 2026 https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/pet-ownership-costs.html and full PDF https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/pet-ownership-costs.pdf (vet inflation 5.5% YoY, vet spending growth about 4x pet-store, 25-30% of practices corporate or PE owned, 95M pet households, $158B spend, deferred care). Legal caveat: state veterinary practice acts restrict diagnosing without a client-patient relationship, so reviewers must stay in price and question-generation territory.
first_30_days: Hire two contract vet techs at an hourly rate. Launch a landing page and post in owner communities and Reddit pet-cost threads with 'send me your estimate and I'll benchmark it free' to collect the first 100 estimates. Build the price table by hand in a spreadsheet, then charge $19 from review number 30. Approach one pet-insurance MGA or employer-benefit broker with the first regional benchmark chart. Target 100 reviews and 30 paid by day 30.

title: Voucher Lease-Up Desk for Soft Markets
one_liner: An ops service that gets units voucher-ready and through housing-authority inspection and paperwork in days, turning Section 8 from a hassle into the cheapest demand source in a soft market.
customer: Mid-size multifamily operators (300-5,000 units) in soft Sun Belt markets with high concessions, with housing authorities and mobility nonprofits as secondary payers.
problem: Apartment List shows 7.0% vacancy, 34 days to lease (longest September since 2019) and concessions on 15.8% of stabilized units (Austin 37%). Yet many operators still avoid Housing Choice Voucher applicants because inspection scheduling and contract paperwork can stretch weeks, costing roughly $300+ of rent a week on a $1,388 median unit. Voucher holders, meanwhile, fail to find units.
solution: A virtual pre-inspection app that walks site staff through HUD's NSPIRE-based checklist with photos so units pass first time. It automates the tenancy-approval and contract packet and tracks status across 50-100 local housing authorities, checks rent-reasonableness and payment standards before pricing, and publishes a live 'voucher-ready units' feed to caseworkers.
why_now: Time-to-lease is at a multi-year high and concessions are replacing rent growth, so landlords will trade a small admin burden for near-guaranteed rent. Authority inspections have moved to one federal standard, which a checklist app can encode.
revenue_model: $350-600 per successful voucher lease-up (against a $1,400 month of vacancy) or $1.50 per unit per month subscription, plus contracts with authorities and mobility programs.
non_obvious_insight: Operators treat vouchers as a risk problem when it is a cycle-time problem, measured in days, which is exactly what a 34-day-to-lease market prices. Government pays most of the rent, so the lowest-CAC tenant class is being left on the table. Housing-authority funding stress is the main risk, so sell to authorities with reserves and use source-of-income laws as a second wedge.
first_30_days: Pick two metros. Call 20 regional managers and offer a free pre-inspection pilot on 10 vacant units. Partner with two authority landlord-liaison offices and one mobility nonprofit. Charge only per lease-up once the unit is under contract with the authority.

title: Inheriting the Lease: Rent-Stabilized Succession Service
angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
one_liner: A service that helps families of rent-regulated elders build and keep the co-residency evidence that lets them inherit a below-market lease, and files the succession claim within days of a death.
customer: Adult children and relatives living with rent-stabilized or rent-controlled elders (about 1M stabilized units in NYC alone, plus SF, LA, Newark and DC). Elder-law and tenant-rights attorneys, senior centers, home-care agencies and hospital discharge planners white-label or refer.
problem: In regulated housing, a family member who can prove co-residency (typically 2 years, or 1 for seniors and the disabled) can succeed to the lease. The lease can be worth six figures over time. Landlords, who gain by re-renting at market, often contest, and the outcome hinges on documents families never assembled while the elder was alive (IDs, tax returns, bills, benefit and medical mail). After death the family faces a notice in weeks, with the elder's records locked in an unopened estate.
solution: Run a lease-inheritance readiness audit and an evidence ledger that collects only genuine documents (address-bearing IDs, filings, bank and medical mail, affidavits from neighbors). After a death, generate a Day-1 succession packet: notice to the landlord, agency filings, and attorney referral. Contested cases go to partner lawyers on contingency or through right-to-counsel programs.
why_now: NYC's political shift toward tenant protection, the SF rent emergency and record middle-income rent distress raise the stakes. The first Boomer tenants are aging out. Good Cause protections and local rent laws expand the leases worth inheriting. AI-generated pleadings are flooding housing courts, which raises the value of clean, verifiable evidence.
revenue_model: $199-399 per family file plus $6-9 per month for the evidence ledger. White-label and per-file fees from law firms, nonprofits and home-care agencies. Referral fees from partner attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: For many urban middle-class families the biggest asset passed at death is not money but a below-market lease, and the value is lost through missing paperwork, not through the law. The $124T wealth-transfer statistics ignore it entirely.
first_30_days: With two elder-law attorneys, draft evidence checklists from the state rent-stabilization rules. Run three clinics at senior centers or tenant associations. Charge $199 for the first 20 pilot families and track landlord responses. Publish a plain-language Succession Readiness Score for tenants.

title: Population-Diverse iPSC Villages for Drug Safety
one_liner: Pool 50-100 genetically diverse donor iPSC lines in one dish and read out each donor's drug response by genotype, giving pharma a 'clinical trial in a dish' for roughly the cost of one experiment.
customer: Pharma safety-pharmacology and toxicology groups, oligonucleotide and gene-editing developers worried about idiosyncratic toxicity, and NAM-adopting CROs.
problem: The NAM debate centers on organ complexity, but single-donor organoids cannot show the population variability behind idiosyncratic liver injury or QT prolongation. FDA now wants 'adequately validated' methods, and conventional multi-donor testing costs n times as much.
solution: A curated, consented and commercially licensable diverse iPSC panel differentiated to cardiomyocytes or neurons (where villages are best proven), dosed with compound series and demultiplexed by genotype through scRNA-seq. Deliver donor-level dose-response distributions, genotype-linked sensitivity and concordance versus clinical outcomes.
why_now: Village-in-a-dish methods have matured, with CIRM-funded pooled iPSC-cardiomyocyte 'clinical trial in a dish' work and a 2026 methods perspective in Frontiers in Bioengineering. Greenstone Biosciences is an early commercial competitor in cardiac models. The FDA rule gives sponsors a reason to buy, and scRNA-seq costs keep falling.
revenue_model: $60-150k per compound panel, $300k/year subscriptions, and licensing the panel to CROs.
non_obvious_insight: Pooling collapses the cost of diversity: n=100 costs roughly what n=5 does. The moat is the consented, well-characterized line panel and a genotype-linked outcomes database, not the assay, which anyone can copy.
first_30_days: License 30-50 lines from public repositories, checking commercial-use consent. Build a cardiomyocyte village. Test 20 reference cardiotoxic and safe drugs and publish the concordance. Pitch 10 safety-pharmacology leads on $30k pilots.

title: Betting Profit-and-Loss Statements for Credit Unions
one_liner: Turn a member's bank ACH data into an 'investment-style' betting P&L (what they recovered per dollar deposited) and optional spending guardrails, licensed per member to credit unions and neobanks.
customer: Community banks, credit unions with young or college-town memberships, and neobanks, paying $0.25-0.60 per member per month. A free consumer version targets Gen Z bettors and their worried parents or partners.
problem: Online betting and prediction-market use is surging among the young. In June-July 2026 first-time users were about 3x January levels. Gen Z and Millennials were 88% of activity (Gen Z 48%). Bettors recovered under 75 cents per dollar sent to platforms. 23% of sports bettors bet daily and 34% weekly. Households that bet had a median deposit balance of only 59% of non-bettors'. Most of these users do not think of themselves as gamblers: 20% of respondents call sports betting a type of investment, Gen Z is about twice as likely to, and buying prediction-market event contracts is more likely to be called an investment than sports betting is.
solution: A detector that classifies ACH and card flows to sportsbooks, sweepstakes casinos and event-contract exchanges, using a maintained list of originator and descriptor names. It produces a plain 'Your realized return: -27%' statement in the vocabulary bettors already use (returns, cost basis), with a monthly summary and opt-in deposit caps or a cooling-off freeze. A parent, partner or co-guardian mode makes it useful for Gen Z members who live at home. The consumer version is a free upload-your-statement tool that generates a shareable 'what's your recovery ratio' card, which doubles as the top of the funnel for credit-union licenses.
why_now: Prediction markets went mainstream in 2026 and the FIFA World Cup drove the June-July spike. Football season, which overlaps other major leagues, starts a new peak now, and first-time users grew 22% YoY in the 2025 football season. Regulators and financial institutions are still working out how to treat event contracts. Under BofA's own framing they sit in a gray zone between entertainment and investing.
revenue_model: B2B: $2-5K/month pilot fees, then $0.25-0.60 per member per month. B2C: free P&L tool, $4.99/month for caps and alerts, and paid family co-guardian seats. Possible later add-on: aggregate, anonymized risk analytics for lenders.
non_obvious_insight: Self-serve gambling blocks fail because bettors do not classify themselves as gamblers, so a harm-reduction message framed as 'gambling addiction' gets ignored, while a return-on-investment statement speaks their mental model. BofA identified betting activity purely from ACH flows, which shows any bank can build the same detection. Working hypothesis, not verified because my search budget ran out: card merchant-category-code blocks used by many banks probably miss ACH-funded prediction-market deposits. Validate with two or three credit-union risk teams before building. Evidence: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/online-betting-platforms.html and its full PDF https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/online-betting-platforms.pdf (3x first-timers, recovery under 75 cents, 88% Gen Z plus Millennials, 20% see betting as investing, 59% median balance).
first_30_days: Week 1: compile a list of ACH originator and descriptor names for major sportsbooks, sweepstakes casinos and event-contract exchanges, and ship a client-side upload-a-CSV P&L calculator with a shareable result card. Week 2: seed it in Gen Z finance and sports-betting subreddits and Discords to collect real recovery-ratio numbers. Week 3: cold-email 30 credit unions near universities and military bases (member-financial-wellness and CUSO contacts) with the anonymized ratio data. Week 4: sign one or two paid pilots at $2-5K/month. Legal review of state gambling-related messaging rules is required before launch.

title: A Suable LLC With Reserves for Every Agent
one_liner: Mass-produced, series-LLC legal wrappers that give each paid agent a registered agent for service of process, a capital reserve, and tax handling, so counterparties have someone to sue.
customer: Indie developers and small studios monetizing paid agents, MCP servers and pay-per-call endpoints (they pay). Enterprise buyers and buying agents use the registry for free. Later, enterprises that want internal agents to contract externally without exposing the parent company.
problem: An agent cannot be sued, hold a bank account or be a contract party. A buyer's counsel asks 'who is my counterparty?' and the honest answer is a 22-year-old with a Discord handle. Sellers, meanwhile, face personal liability and VAT/sales-tax obligations across dozens of jurisdictions from micro-sales made without any human checkout.
solution: One low-cost Delaware or Wyoming series-LLC cell per agent, created in batch: registered agent, EIN, bank or stablecoin account, and a mandatory reserve (say $500-5,000) held in T-bills. The agent's public key is registered so any counterparty can resolve key to entity to reserve balance to claims history. Buying agents can enforce a rule such as 'reserve at least 20x order size'. An embedded merchant-of-record partner handles VAT and sales tax, and an optional insurance rider covers errors.
why_now: x402-style stablecoin micro-payments let agents sell without any human checkout. Legal commentators in 2026 are publishing playbooks for wrapping autonomous agents in LLCs (for example Aaron Wright's essay on the agent's legal body and Ledger's work on registered AI entities). Regimes such as California's have made 'the AI did it' no defense, so buyers now want a named responsible entity.
revenue_model: $49 per agent per month plus $99 formation fee, yield on pooled reserves (roughly 4% on float), 1% merchant-of-record fee, and insurance commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Identity is the wrong primitive. Strangers trust each other when the counterparty has something to lose and somewhere a summons can be served, which is exactly what corporations were invented to provide. The reserve is the product and the reputation score is a byproduct. Caveat: veil-piercing and principal liability still apply, so the product must be candid that it makes agents serviceable and collateralized, not judgment-proof.
first_30_days: Partner with a registered-agent firm and one series-LLC attorney. Offer 50 founding 'agent cells' to MCP and paid-endpoint developers via developer communities and X. Handle paperwork in manual batches. Validate demand by getting two enterprise buyers to say they will only purchase from agents with a registered entity and reserve.

title: Dead-Zone Analytics to Price Satellite Add-Ons
one_liner: A tool that finds the small share of subscribers who will pay for satellite coverage, and prices it for them.
customer: Regional and mid-size mobile network operators and MVNOs launching satellite-to-phone services.
problem: Satellite-mobile partnerships are multiplying, but 'key questions remain unresolved' (Satellite Today, Sept 2026): carriers do not know how to price or differentiate them, and European operators disagree on their value. Giving the service away destroys value.
solution: Software that runs inside the operator's data environment and computes per-subscriber out-of-coverage dwell time and travel patterns. It segments buyers, runs price and offer experiments, and measures incremental ARPU and churn. It also tells network planners where satellite fills gaps more cheaply than a new site.
why_now: Deals with SpaceX, AST and others are now signed in bulk. Operators need to justify them commercially. SpaceX holds its own spectrum, which raises the stakes for carrier differentiation.
revenue_model: Revenue share of 5-10% of incremental add-on revenue, or a $/subscriber-year fee. Fixed-fee analytics packages for smaller operators.
non_obvious_insight: The value of satellite coverage is concentrated in perhaps 5-10% of subscribers who spend real time outside coverage (rural, hunters, truckers, boaters). Pricing to them beats a blanket giveaway.
first_30_days: Sign one regional operator as a design partner. Run a free 60-day retrospective on anonymized coverage and dwell data, and show the segment size and revenue case. Convert to a pilot on real offers.

title: Cooler-Door Pivot for THC Beverage Brands
one_liner: A 45-day pivot studio that moves hemp-THC drink and gummy brands into compliant functional products under their existing distributor and retailer slots, plus a per-container THC ledger for distributors and retailers.
customer: Small and mid-size hemp-THC beverage and edible brands, beverage distributors including alcohol-licensed ones, and convenience, liquor and smoke-shop chains holding hemp SKUs. Brands pay for the pivot sprint and co-pack. Distributors and retailers pay a subscription for the SKU ledger.
problem: P.L. 119-37 redefines hemp to 0.4 mg total THC per container. The effective date was pushed from Nov 12 to Dec 11, 2026 by H.R. 6500 (signed Sept 2), while synthetic cannabinoids lose hemp status on Nov 12. The US Hemp Roundtable estimates about 95% of existing products fall outside the new definition, and a typical THC drink has 2-10 mg per can. There is no federal sell-through safe harbor. The industry employs about 350,000 people. Distributors are asking whether alcohol-licensed wholesalers can even accept returns in three-tier states, and operators face a liquidity problem, not a compliance problem.
solution: Two parts. First, an SKU ledger where COAs and pack volumes are converted into per-container total THC (delta-9 plus decarboxylated THCA) and a keep, pull or return status by state, with vendor chargeback letters and a documented disposition trail. Second, a pivot studio that reuses the brand's flavor systems, cans and design to launch adaptogen, functional or non-alcoholic SKUs through a vetted co-packer, so the brand keeps its distributor agreements and planogram slots. An optional bridge licenses the brand to a state-licensed cannabis producer, since licensed dispensaries are unaffected by the federal redefinition.
why_now: The reprieve to Dec 11 gives roughly 10 weeks. Four congressional frameworks are pending: Barr, Van Duyne and Landsman, Comer, and a Sheehy-Klobuchar Senate companion. The ledger works whether Congress bans or regulates, because age-21, testing and labeling regimes would still need lab-verified per-container data. Retailers and distributors are already telling counsel to audit inventory and plan wind-downs, and gummy prices are reported at 30-50% of 2025 levels.
revenue_model: $5-15k fixed fee per brand pivot sprint, plus a 2-5% royalty or co-pack margin on the pivot SKUs. $199-499 per month per distributor or retail chain for the SKU ledger and chargeback tooling. Finder fee on brand-licensing deals to licensed operators.
non_obvious_insight: As Harris Sliwoski puts it, 'The problem for many operators will not be compliance but liquidity' (https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/what-the-2026-federal-hemp-ban-means-for-unsold-hemp-inventory/). The scarce asset of a THC-drink brand is not inventory, which is illiquid and repricing downward, but its cooler-door slots and distributor agreements, which are among the hardest things to win in beverages. Those slots vanish if the brand disappears. The per-container standard turns an impossible reformulation into a category switch: LearnBrands notes the demand is being inherited by non-alcoholic beer, alcohol-removed wine and functional beverages (https://www.learnbrands.com/post/hemp-thc-beverage-ban-november-2026). Sources on the reprieve and stakes: https://foleyhoag.com/news-and-insights/blogs/cannabis-and-the-law/2026/september/a-temporary-reprieve-for-hemp-thc-products%E2%80%A6-but-what-now/ and https://www.ediblerank.com/legal/hemp-ban-timeline
first_30_days: Pull 40 THC-beverage brands from distributor and retailer press lists and offer a free exposure scan built from their COAs and volumes. Sell three paid pivot sprints. Line up one co-packer with non-alcoholic and adaptogen capability. Pilot the SKU ledger with two distributors and one c-store chain, producing their pull and return list.

title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.

title: TurkBridge: MTurk-Compatible Verified-Human Marketplace
one_liner: An MTurk requester-API-compatible endpoint backed by an identity-verified, proof-of-human worker pool, launched as Amazon Mechanical Turk closes on 30 Sept 2026.
customer: Academic labs and survey researchers, small ML data-labeling teams, and apps that use human-in-the-loop micro-tasks through boto3 or psiTurk-style code. Displaced MTurk workers are the supply side.
problem: Amazon closes MTurk on 30 Sept 2026 and the FAQ names no alternatives or migration path. New HITs end 30 Sept, bonuses are possible until 30 Oct, and transaction history is inaccessible after 28 Jan 2027. SageMaker Ground Truth and Augmented AI lose the MTurk worker type on the same date. Requesters have legacy code and no drop-in replacement, and quality was already collapsing because workers submitted AI output. One HN user says their app 'has been using Amazon Mechanical Turk for left-pad queries, and that service is shutting down in less than two weeks.'
solution: (1) Publish an API shim that mimics the MTurk requester operations (CreateHIT, ListAssignmentsForHIT, ApproveAssignment, qualification requirements, sandbox), so a codebase migrates by changing an endpoint URL. (2) Build supply from ex-MTurk workers on Turkopticon and worker forums, who lose income on the closure date. Give each worker a verified unique-person identity, passkey and liveness checks, and behavioural anti-LLM signals. (3) Sell two tiers, 'verified human' and 'domain expert', with paid-per-task quality gates. The product is the proof that a human did the work, priced above the old race-to-the-bottom rate.
why_now: The shutdown date is two days away, and worker income disappears the same day. Generic open crowd platforms have been wrecked by LLMs, so verified humanness has become the scarce good. Identity-verification APIs are now cheap (Didit, 'Stripe for Identity Verification', launched on HN in March 2026).
revenue_model: A 20-30% take on task payments, a $99/mo lab plan with participant-screening tools, and a per-verification fee for enterprise annotation buyers.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust in who is doing the task, and the API compatibility is what lets you take the customers. The MTurk FAQ confirms the dates and lists no alternative or migration path (https://www.mturk.com/help). In the 534-point HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49457545), dubeye writes: 'The problem as I see it is verifying the work is not done by AI. If it was possible to verify somehow that the work is definitely not done by AI I think there would still be a market.' Another user found MNIST accuracy from Ground Truth on MTurk 'marginally better than guessing.' Prolific is named as the maintained alternative, but I found no evidence that any alternative offers MTurk API compatibility. Legacy scripts are the switching cost, and the shim removes it.
first_30_days: Week 1: write the shim covering the 6 most-used MTurk operations, using boto3's endpoint_url override. Post a 'migrate in 10 minutes' guide on r/mturk, psiTurk and academic Twitter. Weeks 2-3: onboard the first 300-500 workers with ID and liveness checks. Recruit 5 lab requesters with free credits in exchange for case studies. Week 4: run paid studies, publish a proof-of-human quality comparison against raw MTurk data, and start charging the take rate.

title: Josephine Reborn: Permit Concierge for Home Kitchens
one_liner: Josephine's home-cooked-meal marketplace was boxed in by health law; California's MEHKO law now licenses home restaurants, so build the permit concierge and a compliant direct-to-consumer storefront, not another marketplace.
customer: Home cooks, especially immigrant and regional-cuisine specialists (tamales, Armenian, Korean, Oaxacan, Filipino), in Los Angeles County and the roughly 19 California jurisdictions that had authorized MEHKOs as of May 2026. Many already sell via Instagram and WhatsApp without a permit.
problem: MEHKO caps are 30 meals/day, 90/week and roughly $107k/year. Applying costs about $597 plus about $347/yr in LA County, plus food-handler certification, menu SOPs, labels, sales logs and inspections. Third-party delivery apps are restricted, so cooks cannot just list on DoorDash. No tool enforces the caps, produces inspector-ready records, or helps neighbors find them, and paperwork is mostly in English.
solution: A permit concierge ($249-399 one-time) that completes the application, SOPs and multilingual allergen labels. Then a $20/mo cook operating system: link-in-bio storefront with pre-orders and pickup windows, automatic sell-out at 30/day and 90/week, temperature and sales logs exported in the county's format, and Stripe payments. Demand comes from neighborhood 'Friday drop' maps and newsletters and workplace pickup clusters. Cooks own their customers; there is no marketplace.
why_now: MEHKO adoption is spreading county by county (17 counties plus Berkeley and Long Beach by May 2026), with LA County running an active program. Restaurant prices are high, social commerce is normal, and AI makes multilingual SOPs and labels nearly free. A few early MEHKO startups exist, so the opening is to be permit-first, multilingual and neighborhood-by-neighborhood.
revenue_model: $249-399 permit concierge fee; $20/mo per cook SaaS; roughly 1% payments margin; affiliate income from food-handler training and liability insurance. Later, a bulk-permitting contract with counties that want cleaner inspection records.
non_obvious_insight: The marketplace was the illegal or unscalable part, and under MEHKO it is structurally limited to direct-to-consumer sales. The scarce asset is the permit, and the winning product is compliance and storefront tooling that turns each cook into her own licensed restaurant. Enforcing the meal caps in software becomes a feature, and it makes the vendor the county health department's preferred partner.
first_30_days: Attend LA County MEHKO office hours. Find 10 cooks on Instagram (#lahomecook, #tamales) and do their applications free in exchange for case studies. Build the storefront with Shopify or Stripe plus a no-code cap rule. Target 5 issued permits within about 60 days, then start charging the $20/mo.

title: Workup Cover: Insurance for Scan Findings
one_liner: A prepaid guarantee sold at checkout for $800-$1,000 whole-body MRIs and $949 cancer blood tests that covers the second read, the guideline triage and pre-priced follow-up when a scan finds something.
customer: Cash-pay screening buyers 45-70 (whole-body MRI, multi-cancer blood tests, coronary calcium, low-dose CT). First, people who already hold a frightening PDF; second, imaging centers and screening brands that want higher conversion and fewer angry customers; third, concierge doctors and employers.
problem: Screening has gotten cheap enough for the middle class (Function Health's Ezra scan lists at $999 or $799 for members, SimonMed at $899 promotional). The FDA advisory panel voted on September 23, 2026 to back Grail's Galleri blood test, and a new law lets Medicare cover such tests starting in 2028. But the tail is unpriced and unmanaged: in one large study about one in three whole-body MRI participants had an incidental finding and 62% of those biopsied had no malignancy, and the American College of Radiology does not recommend total-body MRI for average-risk adults. The follow-up (specialist visits, repeat imaging, biopsy) is stressful, uncoordinated and can run into the thousands.
solution: An add-on with three layers. (1) A subspecialty radiologist second read within 48 hours. (2) Guideline-based triage (Bosniak, TI-RADS, Fleischner, LI-RADS) that turns the majority of low-risk findings into 'do nothing or repeat in 12 months' with a written explanation. (3) A nurse navigator who books any needed follow-up at pre-negotiated cash prices and, once loss data exist, a financial cap on follow-up costs underwritten with a reinsurer or managing general agent. Phase 1 has no underwriting: sell 'Second Read and Triage' for $149 standalone; Phase 2 adds the guarantee.
why_now: Three things converged in 2025-26: scan prices fell below $1,000 through Function Health and others, the first FDA advisory-panel endorsement of a multi-cancer blood test arrived, and Medicare coverage is scheduled for 2028. Volume of consumer screening is climbing while incidental-finding anxiety is a top complaint in patient communities.
revenue_model: $149-249 attach fee at time of scan purchase (screening seller keeps 20-30% revenue share), $199 standalone second reads, and reinsured guarantee margin: most findings resolve with a read, so expected follow-up payout per member is a small fraction of the fee. Later: protocol licensing to health systems and imaging chains.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to mass preventive screening is not the price of the test but the unpriced tail. Pricing the tail like an extended warranty turns screening's biggest ethical objection (cascades of follow-up) into a product feature, and it lets cheap scans sell without the seller being blamed for the aftermath. A radiology-native underwriter also prices this risk better than a generic insurer.
first_30_days: Recruit three moonlighting subspecialty teleradiologists licensed in target states and one RN navigator. Set up secure image upload with an off-the-shelf DICOM-sharing platform. Launch a $149 'Scary PDF Second Read' in the patient communities around Prenuvo and Function, and sign referral agreements with two independent imaging centers selling $899 MRIs. Log every finding and outcome to price the guarantee. Target 100 second reads in 60 days.

title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.

title: Surety-Bonded License Plates for AI Agents
one_liner: A registrar that binds each autonomous agent to a legally accountable, insured principal through a surety bond and a revocable credential merchants and platforms can check.
customer: Agent developers and vendors that need acceptance by merchants, booking and B2B procurement platforms, the merchants and platforms that want to admit agents safely, and surety insurers or MGAs.
problem: Visa, Mastercard and Amex are activating agent payments in 2026, but dispute and liability infrastructure barely exists. Merchants bear the chargebacks, and Mastercard is reportedly planning scheme-carried liability for certified agents. Identity schemes such as Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Cloudflare's signed agents say who an agent is, but not who pays when it misbehaves.
solution: Register the agent and underwrite it with a test suite, spend caps and a behaviour policy. Issue a signed credential with a visible bond limit, and let merchants and platforms verify it with one API call. A claims process pays merchants for agent-caused losses, and violations revoke the credential. Start with an MGA and fronting-carrier partnership.
why_now: Card networks are moving on agent payments in 2026, Lloyd's-backed AI liability covers launched in 2025, and merchants are asking who is liable for agent orders. Signed-agent identity standards exist, so the missing layer is accountability.
revenue_model: Annual premium of 1-5% of bond limit, a registration fee, and float on the claims reserve.
non_obvious_insight: Identity without liability is theatre. The mature trust machine for strangers who might not pay is suretyship (contractor licences, notary bonds), not a reputation score, and a bond turns 'trust me' into a price.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical (restaurant and hotel booking, or B2B procurement agents). Sign five agent developers, secure a letter of intent from a surety or MGA, build the underwriting test suite, and get three merchants to trial a bonded-only allowlist.
